newsitem.title: LEBANON: Protesters demonstrate outside Lebanese parliament.
newsitem.headline: Protesters demonstrate outside Lebanese parliament.

text.p: Protesters demonstrated outside the Lebanese parliament on Monday against a government law that will close private radio and television stations and leave only a handful that are owned by establishment figures.

The demonstrations by some 100 students and media workers took place as parliament began a three-day debate on the policy statement of the new government of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri which will be followed by a vote of confidence.
"No nation without freedom of expression," said one protester banner. "No to censorship," said another.
A dozen soldiers watched but did not intervene since the demonstration was authorised by parliament Speaker Nabih Berri despite a three-year-old ban imposed by Hariri on all public demonstrations.
The new law will shut scores of private radio and television stations on November 30 and licence only a handful of stations, mostly owned by establishment figures including Hariri.
Former prime minister Selim al-Hoss opened the parliamentary debate by saying Lebanon's public administration and political life were riddled with corruption.

He cited as an example a Reuters report during last summer's parliamentary elections that Hariri supporters were seen by a reporter in Beirut paying some voters 100,000 Lebanese pounds ($64) to vote for him.

The government's policy statement puts new emphasis on social policies -- housing, transportation, medicare and social security -- and development of agriculture, industry and tourism after years of heavy spending on infrastructure projects.
Hariri, whose multi-billion dollars projects have strained Lebanon's financial resources, is facing growing demands to pay more attention to the needs of the poor.

A broad spectrum of opposition groups, labour unions and media workers have called a one-day general strike and demonstration on Thursday to protest against the closure of radio and television stations, the permanent ban on street demonstrations and the government's social policies.
